summary.title: Software Testing Anti-patterns
summary.one_liner: You learn 13 technology-agnostic software testing anti-patterns, such as relying only on unit or only on integration tests, and why each one hurts.
keywords: why you need both unit and integration tests
takeaways: Unit tests and integration tests are complementary; relying on only one kind is a common anti-pattern.
Integration tests catch problems unit tests cannot, such as database transactions, triggers, contracts between modules, and performance.
The right test mix depends on the application: command-line tools lean on unit tests, payment systems on integration tests, and UI-heavy apps on UI tests.
Test the most business-critical functionality first rather than chasing code coverage numbers or trivial tests of the data model.
Integration tests are slower and harder to debug, so a feedback loop built only on them is expensive.
summary.summary: This article by Kostis Kapelonis catalogs high-level, technology-agnostic software testing anti-patterns, using the test pyramid as its terminology base. It defines unit tests and integration tests with a rule of thumb for telling them apart, then lists 13 anti-patterns ordered roughly by how often they appear. The first anti-patterns are covered in depth with worked examples: a cyclomatic-complexity comparison of unit versus integration test counts, run-time estimates, and debugging scenarios. Further examples show how the ideal test mix changes by application type. The page is cut off partway through the section on testing the wrong functionality, so the remaining anti-patterns are not covered in the text provided.
